claim: Cytoplasmic dynein is the predominant minus-end-directed microtubule (MT) motor in most eukaryotic cells.
source: Cytoplasmic dynein is the predominant minus-end-directed microtubule (MT) motor in most eukaryotic cells.
evidence: This is a statement of established scientific knowledge about dynein's role in cells.

claim: Dynein crosslinks and slides anti-parallel MTs in vitro.
source: Here we demonstrate that dynein crosslinks and slides anti-parallel MTs in vitro.
evidence: This is a primary finding directly stated and supported by experimental data shown in the manuscript.

claim: A minimal dimeric motor lacking a tail domain and associated subunits can cause MT sliding.
source: Surprisingly, a minimal dimeric motor lacking a tail domain and associated subunits can cause MT sliding.
evidence: This finding is supported by experimental data with GST-Dyn1331kDa shown in Figure 1F and related experiments.

claim: Motors pause and frequently reverse direction when encountering an anti-parallel MT overlap.
source: Single molecule imaging reveals that motors pause and frequently reverse direction when encountering an anti-parallel MT overlap, suggesting that the two motor domains can bind both MTs simultaneously.
evidence: This is supported by single molecule tracking data shown in Figure 4.

claim: The two motor domains can bind both MTs simultaneously.
source: Single molecule imaging reveals that motors pause and frequently reverse direction when encountering an anti-parallel MT overlap, suggesting that the two motor domains can bind both MTs simultaneously.
evidence: This is inferred from the pausing and directional reversal behavior observed in single molecule experiments.

claim: In the mitotic spindle, inward microtubule sliding by dynein counteracts outward sliding generated by kinesin-5.
source: In the mitotic spindle, inward microtubule sliding by dynein counteracts outward sliding generated by kinesin-5, and we show that a tailless, dimeric motor is sufficient to drive this activity in mammalian cells.
evidence: This is supported by in vivo experiments shown in Figure 5 and cited literature.

claim: A tailless, dimeric motor is sufficient to drive inward sliding activity in mammalian cells.
source: In the mitotic spindle, inward microtubule sliding by dynein counteracts outward sliding generated by kinesin-5, and we show that a tailless, dimeric motor is sufficient to drive this activity in mammalian cells.
evidence: This is demonstrated by experiments with GST-hDyn in Figure 5.

claim: Cytoplasmic dynein is a 1.2 MDa, multisubunit microtubule motor complex that belongs to the AAA family of molecular machines.
source: Cytoplasmic dynein is a 1.2 MDa, multisubunit microtubule motor complex that belongs to the AAA family of molecular machines (Ogura and Wilkinson, 2001; Allan, 2011).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: The dynein complex is composed of a dimer of two heavy chains.
source: The dynein complex is composed of a dimer of two heavy chains.
evidence: This is established structural knowledge about dynein.

claim: Each heavy chain contains a C-terminal motor domain and an N-terminal tail domain that binds to accessory chains and adaptor proteins.
source: Each heavy chain contains a C-terminal motor domain, and an N-terminal tail domain that binds to accessory chains and adaptor proteins, which are needed to link the motor to its cargo (Kardon and Vale, 2009).
evidence: This is established structural and functional knowledge supported by citation.

claim: Dynein transports a plethora of cargoes towards MT minus-ends, including many types of organelles, mRNAs and proteins.
source: Dynein transports a plethora of cargoes towards MT minus-ends, including many types of organelles, mRNAs and proteins.
evidence: This is established knowledge about dynein's cargo transport function.

claim: When mammalian cells enter mitosis, dynein is needed to remodel the prophase MT network.
source: When mammalian cells enter mitosis, dynein is needed to remodel the prophase MT network (Rusan et al., 2002), and at later stages dynein assists in organizing MTs to form focused spindle poles (Heald et al., 1996; Merdes et al., 1996).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: At later stages of mitosis, dynein assists in organizing MTs to form focused spindle poles.
source: When mammalian cells enter mitosis, dynein is needed to remodel the prophase MT network (Rusan et al., 2002), and at later stages dynein assists in organizing MTs to form focused spindle poles (Heald et al., 1996; Merdes et al., 1996).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Dynein generates an inward force within the spindle that counteracts an outward force generated by kinesin-5 and kinesin-12 motors.
source: Dynein also generates an inward force within the spindle that counteracts an outward force generated by kinesin-5 and kinesin-12 motors (Mitchison et al., 2005; Tanenbaum et al., 2008, 2009; Ferenz et al., 2009; Vanneste et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior literature.

claim: The balance of forces between dynein and kinesins is important for normal spindle assembly.
source: The balance of these forces is important for normal spindle assembly (Tanenbaum and Medema, 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: In cell extracts, dynein has been shown to organize MTs into aster-like structures.
source: In cell extracts, dynein also has been shown to organize MTs into aster-like structures (Verde et al., 1991; Gaglio et al., 1996), drive the fusion of two closely positioned spindles into a single bipolar spindle (Gatlin et al., 2009), and transport stabilized MT seeds to the spindle pole (Heald et al., 1996).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Dynein drives the fusion of two closely positioned spindles into a single bipolar spindle.
source: In cell extracts, dynein also has been shown to organize MTs into aster-like structures (Verde et al., 1991; Gaglio et al., 1996), drive the fusion of two closely positioned spindles into a single bipolar spindle (Gatlin et al., 2009), and transport stabilized MT seeds to the spindle pole (Heald et al., 1996).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: Dynein transports stabilized MT seeds to the spindle pole.
source: In cell extracts, dynein also has been shown to organize MTs into aster-like structures (Verde et al., 1991; Gaglio et al., 1996), drive the fusion of two closely positioned spindles into a single bipolar spindle (Gatlin et al., 2009), and transport stabilized MT seeds to the spindle pole (Heald et al., 1996).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: Purified rat brain dynein induces the formation of large bundles of purified MTs.
source: We similarly found that purified rat brain dynein induces the formation of large bundles of purified MTs (Figure 1A–D).
evidence: This is directly observed in experiments shown in Figure 1A-D.

claim: Addition of ATP induces red MTs to slide within bundles relative to stationary green biotin-MTs.
source: Addition of ATP into the assay chamber induced the red MTs to slide within the bundles relative to the stationary green biotin-MTs (Figure 1E; Video 1).
evidence: This is directly observed in experiments shown in Figure 1E and Video 1.

claim: GST-Dyn1331kDa crosslinked MTs, while a monomeric version lacking the GST dimerizing domain did not.
source: GST-Dyn1331kDa crosslinked MTs, while a monomeric version lacking the GST dimerizing domain did not (Figure 1A–C).
evidence: This is directly observed in experiments shown in Figure 1A-C.

claim: GST-Dyn1331kDa motor induced sliding of MTs within bundles when ATP was added.
source: Similar to rat brain dynein, the GST-Dyn1331kDa motor induced sliding of MTs within the bundles, when ATP was added (Figure 1F; Video 2).
evidence: This is directly observed in experiments shown in Figure 1F and Video 2.

claim: MT sliding does not require dynein associated subunits or any potential second MT binding domain in the dynein heavy chain tail domain.
source: These results provide the first direct in vitro demonstration that cytoplasmic dynein can slide MTs within bundles. They also reveal that sliding does not require dynein associated subunits or any potential second MT binding domain in the dynein heavy chain tail domain.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that GST-Dyn1331kDa, which lacks the tail domain and associated subunits, can still slide MTs.

claim: GST-Dyn1331kDa drove robust sliding of transport MTs along immobilized track MTs.
source: After addition of ATP, GST-Dyn1331kDa drove robust sliding of transport MTs along the immobilized track MTs (Figure 2A, Video 3).
evidence: This is directly observed in experiments shown in Figure 2A and Video 3.

claim: The speed of MT-MT sliding by GST-Dyn1331kDa (53 ± 24 nm/s) was similar to the velocity observed in MT gliding assays (47 ± 11 nm/s).
source: The speed of MT-MT sliding (53 ± 24 nm/s; mean ± SD; Figure 2A) was similar to the velocity observed in MT gliding assays (47 ± 11 nm/s; Figure 2A) with this dynein construct.
evidence: This is quantified from experimental data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Purified rat brain dynein produced MT-MT sliding, although the movement was slower than surface gliding (10 ± 5 nm/s vs 615 ± 200 nm/s).
source: We found that purified rat brain dynein also produced MT-MT sliding using this same assay, although the movement was slower than surface gliding (10 ± 5 nm/s vs 615 ± 200 nm/s) and characterized by more frequent pausing than MT gliding by surface-bound brain dynein (Figure 2B, Video 4).
evidence: This is quantified from experimental data shown in Figure 2B and Video 4.

claim: The large majority of MT sliding events involved MTs in an anti-parallel configuration (18 of 21 events).
source: These experiments revealed that the large majority of MT sliding events involved MTs in an anti-parallel configuration (18 of 21 events, Figure 2C).
evidence: This is quantified from polarity-marked MT experiments shown in Figure 2C.

claim: In 21 of 22 cases analyzed using single GFP-tagged dynein motors, the transport and track MTs were anti-parallel to one another.
source: To confirm this, we also analyzed MT polarity using the direction of movement of single GFP-tagged dynein motors on the track and transport MT, in cases where the transport MT moved past the end of the track MT. In 21 of 22 cases, the transport and track MTs were anti-parallel to one another.
evidence: This is quantified from single molecule tracking experiments.

claim: Purified Dyn1387kD sedimented at approximately 19S in sucrose gradients.
source: In sucrose gradients, purified Dyn1387kD sedimented at approximately 19S (Figure 3C), which is similar in size to the full dynein complex (Paschal et al., 1987), as well as a truncated dimeric dynein (Trokter et al., 2012).
evidence: This is directly observed in sucrose gradient experiments shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Single molecule assays revealed robust processive motion of Dyn1387kD along microtubules with an average speed of 75 ± 40 nm/s.
source: Consistent with it being a dimer, single molecule assays revealed robust processive motion of Dyn1387kD along microtubules with an average speed of 75 ± 40 nm/s (n = 95) (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is quantified from single molecule tracking experiments shown in Figure 3D.

claim: Dyn1387kD bundled MTs in the absence of ATP.
source: Dyn1387kD bundled MTs in the absence of ATP (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A), demonstrating that it can crosslink MTs, similar to GST-Dyn1331kD.
evidence: This is directly observed in experiments shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Addition of ATP to MT bundles with Dyn1387kD resulted in MT sliding.
source: Addition of ATP to MT bundles resulted in MT sliding of MTs in the bundle (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B; Video 5).
evidence: This is directly observed in experiments shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1B and Video 5.

claim: Dyn1387kD drove efficient MT-MT sliding in single MT overlaps, at comparable speeds to its surface gliding motility.
source: Similarly, Dyn1387kD drove efficient MT-MT sliding in single MT overlaps, at comparable speeds to its surface gliding motility (Figure 3G; Video 6).
evidence: This is directly observed and quantified in experiments shown in Figure 3G and Video 6.

claim: Dyn1387kD ΔMTBD showed no specific association with MTs in a cosedimentation assay.
source: Dyn1387kD ΔMTBD showed no specific association with MTs in a cosedimentation assay (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C,D) and was unable to crosslink MTs (Figure 3—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: This is directly observed in cosedimentation experiments shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1C,D.

claim: Dyn1387kD ΔMTBD was unable to crosslink MTs.
source: Dyn1387kD ΔMTBD showed no specific association with MTs in a cosedimentation assay (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C,D) and was unable to crosslink MTs (Figure 3—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: This is directly observed in experiments shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1E.

claim: Dyn1387kD does not possess a MT binding region outside of the motor domain.
source: Thus, Dyn1387kD ΔMTBD does not possess a MT binding region outside of the motor domain.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that deletion of the canonical MTBD eliminates MT binding.

claim: A natively dimerized dynein can crosslink and slide MTs in vitro without associated chains or an additional MT binding site.
source: Together, these results show that a natively dimerized dynein can crosslink and slide MTs in vitro, and that associated chains or an additional MT binding site is not required for this activity.
evidence: This is concluded from experiments with Dyn1387kD and Dyn1387kD ΔMTBD.

claim: Individual TMR-labeled GST-Dyn1331kDa moved unidirectionally and highly processively on single MTs.
source: As expected from prior work (Reck-Peterson et al., 2006), individual TMR-labeled GST-Dyn1331kDa moved unidirectionally and highly processively on single MTs.
evidence: This is observed in single molecule experiments and consistent with prior literature.

claim: GST-Dyn1331kDa appeared largely immobile in MT overlaps.
source: However, GST-Dyn1331kDa appeared largely immobile in MT overlaps (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is directly observed in single molecule experiments shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Individual dynein molecules moving processively along a single MT would appear to stop moving when they reached the MT overlap zone.
source: Interestingly, when individual molecules moving processively along a single MT reached the MT overlap zone, they would appear to stop moving (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is directly observed in single molecule tracking experiments shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Individual dynein molecules were not completely immobile in MT overlap zones, but rather frequently moved bidirectionally with long pauses between each run.
source: However, when individual molecules were tracked with ∼10 nm precision, it was apparent that individual dynein molecules were not completely immobile in MT overlap zones, but rather frequently moved bidirectionally with long pauses between each run (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is observed in high-resolution single molecule tracking experiments shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Long distance directional switching and frequent prolonged pausing were never observed when dynein moved along single MTs.
source: While yeast dynein occasionally takes backwards steps (Reck-Peterson et al., 2006), such long distance directional switching and frequent prolonged pausing were never observed when dynein moved along single MTs (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is observed by comparing dynein behavior on single MTs vs. in overlaps, as shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Single dynein molecules moved unidirectionally and processively on single MTs coated with high concentrations of GFP-Ase1.
source: Despite the high concentration of GFP-Ase1, single dynein molecules moved unidirectionally and processively (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is directly observed in experiments shown in Figure 4D.

claim: Bidirectional switching and pausing are due to the presence of a MT overlap, not to the presence of GFP-Ase1 on MTs.
source: Thus, we conclude that bidirectional switching and pausing are due to the presence of a MT overlap, not to the presence of GFP-Ase1 on MTs.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that high concentrations of Ase1 on single MTs do not affect dynein motility.

claim: Full-length yeast dynein (Dyn1) showed processive, unidirectional motility along single MTs but transitioned to frequent bidirectional switching and pausing within MT overlaps.
source: Dyn1 showed processive, unidirectional motility along single MTs (Figure 4E), but transitioned to frequent bidirectional switching and pausing within MT overlaps (Figure 4E).
evidence: This is directly observed in single molecule experiments shown in Figure 4E.

claim: The two motor domains of the dynein dimer can bind to the same MT track in a compact, side-by-side configuration and exhibit persistent unidirectional motion.
source: The two motor domains of the dimer can bind to the same MT track, most likely in a compact, side-by-side configuration of the two AAA ring domains (Cho and Vale, 2012), and exhibit persistent unidirectional motion.
evidence: This is inferred from the observed processive motion on single MTs and supported by citation.

claim: The two motor domains can bind to neighboring MTs within a MT overlap and produce a force that acts to slide the two MTs relative to each other.
source: Alternatively, they can bind to neighboring MTs within a MT overlap and produce a force that acts to slide the two MTs relative to each other (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is inferred from the observed behavior in MT overlaps and the sliding activity.

claim: In human cells, kinesin-5 and kinesin-12 motors promote spindle bipolarity by generating an outward force within the spindle.
source: In human cells, kinesin-5, and kinesin-12 motors promote spindle bipolarity by generating an outward force within the spindle (Blangy et al., 1995; Tanenbaum et al., 2009; Vanneste et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: In the absence of both kinesin-5 and kinesin-12, a dynein-dependent inward force causes the rapid collapse of the metaphase spindle to a monopolar structure.
source: In the absence of both kinesins, a dynein-dependent inward force causes the rapid collapse of the metaphase spindle to a monopolar structure (Tanenbaum et al., 2008, 2009; Ferenz et al., 2009; Vanneste et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: GST-hDyn lacks the consensus binding sites for other dynein subunits.
source: GST-hDyn lacks the consensus binding sites for other dynein subunits (Vallee et al., 2012), which we confirmed by immunoprecipitation (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is confirmed by immunoprecipitation experiments shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1A and supported by citation.

claim: When expressed in HEK293 cells, GST-hDyn partially localized to the spindle.
source: When expressed in HEK293 cells, GST-hDyn partially localized to the spindle (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B), indicating that it is a functional MT-binding protein.
evidence: This is directly observed in immunofluorescence experiments shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1B.

claim: GST-hDyn expression substantially increased the number of monopolar spindles in dynein-depleted, kinesin-5 inhibited cells.
source: Strikingly, GST-hDyn expression substantially increased the number of monopolar spindles in dynein-depleted, kinesin-5 inhibited cells (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is quantified from cell-based experiments shown in Figure 5B.

claim: GST-hDyn can recapitulate the inward force normally produced by endogenous dynein.
source: These results reveal that GST-hDyn can recapitulate the inward force, normally produced by the endogenous dynein, providing further support that the motor domains alone are sufficient for this function.
evidence: This is inferred from the rescue experiments showing GST-hDyn can substitute for endogenous dynein.

claim: In metaphase-arrested cells expressing GST-hDyn, kinesin-5 inhibition resulted in 88 ± 2% of cells with monopolar spindles compared to 38 ± 5% in control cells.
source: However, in metaphase-arrested cells expressing GST-hDyn, kinesin-5 inhibition resulted in a much greater percentage (88 ± 2%) of cells with monopolar spindles (Figure 5C,D).
evidence: This is quantified from cell-based experiments shown in Figure 5C,D.

claim: Expression of FKBP-hDyn in the absence of AP20187 did not alter the fraction of monopolar spindles (47.8 ± 2.7%).
source: Expression of FKBP-hDyn in the absence of AP20187 did not alter the fraction of monopolar spindles (47.8 ± 2.7%; mean ± SD), indicating that the monomeric version of dynein was unable to reconstitute the function of native dynein.
evidence: This is quantified from cell-based experiments.

claim: Addition of AP20187 to cells expressing FKBP-hDyn substantially increased the fraction of cells with monopolar spindles to 75.5 ± 2.5%.
source: However, addition of AP20187 to cells expressing FKBP-hDyn substantially increased in the fraction of cells with monopolar spindles (Figure 5E, 75.5 ± 2.5%).
evidence: This is quantified from cell-based experiments shown in Figure 5E.

claim: Dimerization of two dynein motor domains robustly activates the ability of dynein to generate an inward force in the spindle.
source: This result demonstrates that dimerization of two dynein motor domains robustly activates the ability of dynein to generate an inward force in the spindle.
evidence: This is inferred from the comparison of monomeric vs. dimerized FKBP-hDyn activity.

claim: Dynein is important for focusing MT minus ends at the spindle pole.
source: In addition to its role in generating an inward force in the spindle, dynein also is important for focusing MT minus ends at the spindle pole (Walczak and Heald, 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: Depletion of dynein increased the percentage of spindles with unfocused poles and detached centrosomes, but this pole focusing defect was not rescued by GST-hDyn.
source: Depletion of dynein increased the percentage of spindles with unfocused poles and detached centrosomes; however, this pole focusing defect was not rescued by GST-hDyn (Figure 5—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is observed in cell-based experiments shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1D.

claim: A minimal dynein is able to generate an inward force in the spindle, which likely involves anti-parallel MT sliding, but is unable to fulfill other mitotic functions of dynein.
source: These results show that a minimal dynein is able to generate an inward force in the spindle, which likely involves anti-parallel MT sliding, but is unable to fulfill other mitotic functions of dynein.
evidence: This is concluded from the observation that GST-hDyn can rescue spindle collapse but not pole focusing.

claim: Kinesin-5 forms a bipolar tetramer of motor domains and crossbridges and slides MTs by this mechanism.
source: Kinesin-5, which forms a bipolar tetramer of motor domains, crossbridges and slides MTs by such a mechanism (Kashina et al., 1996; Kapitein et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Several classes of kinesin utilize a mechanism involving a secondary MT binding domain for crosslinking and sliding MTs.
source: Several classes of kinesin utilize a similar mechanism for crosslinking and sliding MTs (Straube et al., 2006; Braun et al., 2009; Fink et al., 2009; Seeger and Rice, 2010; Su et al., 2011; Weaver et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior literature.

claim: There is currently no evidence suggesting that cytoplasmic dynein contains a secondary MT binding site outside of the motor domain.
source: However, there is currently no evidence suggesting that cytoplasmic dynein contains a secondary MT binding site outside of the motor domain.
evidence: This is a statement about the lack of prior evidence in the literature.

claim: Previous work has reported that purified brain cytoplasmic dynein crosslinks and bundles MTs.
source: Previous work has reported that purified brain cytoplasmic dynein crosslinks and bundles MTs (Amos, 1989; Toba and Toyoshima, 2004), but the mechanism has remained unclear.
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: The mechanism by which dynein crosslinks and bundles MTs has remained unclear.
source: Previous work has reported that purified brain cytoplasmic dynein crosslinks and bundles MTs (Amos, 1989; Toba and Toyoshima, 2004), but the mechanism has remained unclear.
evidence: This is a statement about the state of knowledge prior to this study.

claim: The transport MTs frequently moved until they reached the end of the track MT, where they swiveled around an end point on the track MT.
source: The transport MTs frequently moved until they reached the end of the track MT, where they swiveled around an end point on the track MT (asterisk Figure 2A).
evidence: This is directly observed in experiments shown in Figure 2A.

claim: The slower motility of rat brain dynein in MT-MT sliding may be a result of the much weaker processivity and directionality observed for individual mammalian dyneins in vitro compared to yeast dynein.
source: The slower motility may be a result of the much weaker processivity and directionality observed for individual mammalian dyneins in vitro compared to yeast dynein (Ross et al., 2006; Cho et al., 2008; Miura et al., 2010; Ori-McKenney et al., 2010; Trokter et al., 2012).
evidence: This is speculated based on prior literature showing differences between mammalian and yeast dynein.

claim: Other proteins such as LIS1 and Ndel1 that directly modify processivity and directionality of mammalian dynein may be needed for more robust processivity and sliding.
source: Other proteins (such as LIS1 and Ndel1) that directly modify these properties of mammalian dynein may be needed for more robust processivity and sliding, consistent with the requirement of these proteins for dynein-dependent MT organization in vivo (Raaijmakers et al., 2013).
evidence: This is speculated based on the known roles of these proteins and supported by citation.

claim: The finding that rat dynein alone is capable of crosslinking and sliding MTs shows that this type of motility is an intrinsic ability of the motor.
source: Nonetheless, the finding that rat dynein alone is capable of crosslinking and sliding MTs in our assays, shows that this type of motility is an intrinsic ability of the motor.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that purified rat dynein can slide MTs without additional factors.

claim: GFP-Ase1 specifically localized to regions of MT overlap.
source: We found that GFP-Ase1 specifically localized to regions of MT overlap (data not shown), as previously described (Loïodice et al., 2005; Yamashita et al., 2005; Janson et al., 2007).
evidence: This is observed in experiments and consistent with prior literature.

claim: Quantitative imaging of MT fluorescence revealed that 2–3 MTs were typically present in each bundle.
source: Quantitative imaging of MT fluorescence revealed that 2–3 MTs were typically present in each bundle.
evidence: This is quantified from imaging experiments.

claim: GFP-Ase1 crosslinks MTs into anti-parallel bundles with an inter-MT spacing of around 15–40 nm.
source: To generate stable anti-parallel overlaps, we crosslinked MTs with GFP-Ase1 (Janson et al., 2007), a protein that crosslinks MTs into anti-parallel bundles with an inter-MT spacing of around 15–40 nm (Gaillard et al., 2008; Roque et al., 2010; Subramanian et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: The inter-MT distance created by Ase1 is within the size range expected for MT crosslinking by a dimeric dynein motor.
source: This inter-MT distance is within the size range expected for MT crosslinking by a dimeric dynein motor (Vallee et al., 1988; Burgess et al., 2003).
evidence: This is inferred from structural information about dynein supported by citations.

claim: Dynein's mechanism for crosslinking and sliding MTs differs from filament sliding mechanisms described for other motor proteins.
source: Our results identify an unexpected mechanism for dynein-driven microtubule sliding, which differs from filament sliding mechanisms described for other motor proteins.
evidence: This is concluded from the comparison of dynein's mechanism with those of kinesins.

claim: Axonemal dyneins use their two motor domains to walk along one MT and employ a second MT binding domain to transport a 'cargo MT'.
source: To generate sliding between two MTs, an individual dynein motor, a dimer of two heavy chains, could use its two motor domains to walk along one MT and employ a second MT binding domain to transport a 'cargo MT'. Axonemal dyneins function in this manner to produce MT sliding in cilia and flagella.
evidence: This is established knowledge about axonemal dynein mechanism.

claim: Cortically-anchored dynein pulls on spindle MTs during spindle positioning.
source: Such a mechanism may also function during spindle positioning, where cortically-anchored dynein pulls on spindle MTs (Galli and van den Heuvel, 2008; Kiyomitsu and Cheeseman, 2012; Kotak et al., 2012; Laan et al., 2012), as well as during centrosome separation, where dynein is anchored to the nuclear envelope (Splinter et al., 2010; Bolhy et al., 2011; Raaijmakers et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior literature.

claim: During centrosome separation, dynein is anchored to the nuclear envelope.
source: Such a mechanism may also function during spindle positioning, where cortically-anchored dynein pulls on spindle MTs (Galli and van den Heuvel, 2008; Kiyomitsu and Cheeseman, 2012; Kotak et al., 2012; Laan et al., 2012), as well as during centrosome separation, where dynein is anchored to the nuclear envelope (Splinter et al., 2010; Bolhy et al., 2011; Raaijmakers et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Anterograde transport of MTs was observed in nerve axons and shown to be dependent upon dynein activity.
source: Anterograde transport of MTs was observed in nerve axons and shown to be dependent upon dynein activity (He et al., 2005), although the mechanism by which dynein moved MTs in the axon was unclear.
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: Loss of dynein in Drosophila neurons results in a loss of uniform MT polarity within axons.
source: Similarly, loss of dynein in Drosophila neurons results in a loss of uniform MT polarity within axons, suggesting that dynein actively sorts MTs based on their polarity (Zheng et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: The mechanism of MT-MT sliding described here provides a model for how dynein may achieve MT sorting in neuronal cells.
source: The mechanism of MT-MT sliding described here provides a model for how dynein may achieve such MT sorting in neuronal cells.
evidence: This is speculated based on the in vitro findings and prior observations in neurons.

claim: Dynein driven MT-MT sliding could be a more generally used mechanism to organize and sort MTs in the cell.
source: Thus, dynein driven MT-MT sliding could be a more generally used mechanism to organize and sort MTs in the cell.
evidence: This is speculated based on the findings of this study.

claim: Kinesin-1 and kinesin-14 utilize a secondary, non-motor, MT binding site located in their tail domains to crosslink and slide MTs.
source: However, these motors either form a tetrameric complex (Kashina et al., 1996; Kapitein et al., 2008), or contain a second MT binding domain within their tail domain, which facilitates MT crosslinking (Jolly et al., 2010) (Figure 6).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature and illustrated in Figure 6.

claim: MT crosslinking and sliding by dynein dimers does not require its tail domain, accessory subunits, regulatory proteins, or further oligomerization.
source: In contrast, our results show that MT crosslinking and sliding by dynein dimers does not require its tail domain, accessory subunits, regulatory proteins, or further oligomerization.
evidence: This is concluded from experiments with minimal dynein constructs.

claim: The two motor domains of dynein likely splay apart, allowing the dimer to bind to two MTs simultaneously.
source: Rather, our results indicate that the two motor domains of a dynein dimer can bind to separate MTs and each motor domain can walk independently on the MT to which it is bound. To accomplish this, the two motor domains likely splay apart, allowing the dimer to bind to the two MTs simultaneously (Figure 6).
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental observations and illustrated in Figure 6.

claim: Recent data suggests that dynein's two motor domains step in a relatively stochastic and independent fashion.
source: Consistent with this notion, recent data suggests that dynein's two motor domains step in a relatively stochastic and independent fashion (DeWitt et al., 2012; Qiu et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to recent literature.

claim: A dynein dimer made of one active and one inactive motor domain still moves processively on a single MT.
